title: They do: -nt
subtitle: Lesson 5 · -nt = they do
intro: So far one person acted at a time: *Puella labōrat*. Today several people act: *Puellae labōrant* 'The girls work.' The verb's **-t** becomes **-nt**, just like *est* becomes *sunt*. New words: three busy verbs – *parat* 'prepares', *portat* 'carries', *spectat* 'looks at' – plus *multae* 'many', *quoque* 'too' and *ubi* 'when, where'.

vocab.notes: *multae puellae* = many girls. For now you use the feminine forms: *multa*, *multam*, *multae*.

example.en: The women get the water ready.

vocab.notes: *videt* = sees; *spectat* = looks at on purpose, watches.

example.en: The women look at the forest.

vocab.notes: *quoque* comes **right after** the word it adds: *Iūlia quoque rīdet* 'Julia laughs too.'

example.en: The girls laugh; the woman laughs too.

example.la: Ubi puellae rīdent, Cornēlia quoque rīdet.
example.en: When the girls laugh, Cornelia laughs too.

grammar.title: -nt = they do
grammar.body:
One girl works: *puella labōrat*. Two girls work: *puellae labōrant*. When the subject is plural, the verb swaps **-t** for **-nt**: **-t** = he / she / it, **-nt** = they.

It works for every verb you know: *stat* → *stant*, *videt* → *vident*, *amat* → *amant*. You already met the same pattern in *est* → *sunt*.

The verb follows its **subject**, not its object: *Puellae aquam portant* 'The girls carry water' – many girls, so -nt, even though there is only one water.

With no noun, the ending alone means 'they': *Rīdent* 'They laugh.'

reading.title: Aqua et puellae
reading.la: Iūlia et Claudia puellae parvae sunt. Nunc aquam portant: via longa est, sed puellae nōn timent. Cornēlia quoque labōrat; terram parat. Ubi puellae Cornēliam vident, rīdent et fēminam vocant. Cornēlia aquam spectat et rīdet. Multae fēminae nunc labōrant, et puellae quoque labōrant. Puellae bonae sunt.
reading.en: Julia and Claudia are little girls. Now they are carrying water: the road is long, but the girls are not afraid. Cornelia is working too; she is preparing the land. When the girls see Cornelia, they laugh and call the woman. Cornelia looks at the water and smiles. Many women are working now, and the girls are working too. The girls are good.
reading.hint: Spot the **-nt** verbs: *portant*, *timent*, *vident*, *rīdent*, *vocant*, *labōrant* – each has a plural subject or simply means 'they'.
